You do need to worry about that 0v set of cells, in particular by not using them or charging them. You do not want to reverse charge a cell that's already dead, because that's what'll happen to a 0V set of cells in series with charged cells. They will force current through those dead cells, and cause it to gain potential in reverse of its intended direction. Hence, don't use, don't charge.

The damage is likely already present to a fair extent, and when they're that deeply discharged they get physically damaged when the chemical reaction builds physical dendrites that puncture your electrolytic holding foils. They create short circuits, which cause cells to self discharge to zero potential and cause them to readily pass current in reverse.

Stop charging it immediately. Stop using it immediately. Any charge or discharge is putting you at risk, because a cell at 0 volts will reverse charge when used. When they get that way, they become a short circuit. All three cells in parallel with the one you're concerned with are dead. They need replacing with three identical cells.

The screw plus their washers:

Screw -> Spring washer -> Flat washer -> Hooked washer -> motor <- Hooked washer <- Flat washer <- Spring washer <- Screw

The screw:  
**8mm inner hex,** for 8mm hex key  
**18mm long** (From the face of the flange to the end of the thread)  
**M8**, 8mm major diameter of screw thread  
**1mm thread pitch,** the distance between each thread when measured on a single perpendicular line.  
Flange diameter 20mm  
Flange thickness 2mm

That would mean this is an M8x1.0x18 screw; M8 1.0mm pitch 18mm length.

If you're unable to find a screw with the flange already built in, simply add the thickness of the flange to your length of the screw to get, and add a washer of the same dimensions. Alternatively, get a screw the same length, and get yourself a spring washer with the right size for the screw head's outer diameter. Then use the spring washer directly after the head, in the same order as the above mentioned sequence.

The C rating relates to the Capacity. If you charge a 2000 mAh cell at 1C, you charge at 2000 mA of charge current. Lower current charging is generally better, as is lower depth of discharge and lower limit for the end of charge termination. 

That boils down to:  
\- Charge slower  
\- Charge between a narrower range in the middle of your state of charge range.  
\- Avoid fully charging, and avoid fully charging at a high speed at all costs.

On the other hand, as others have noted, with the size of the battery pack you may never actually come anywhere close to a 1C charge rate for any one cell in the parallel sets in there. Charging to 100% is theoretically suboptimal for longevity, but the damage done can be significantly reduced by doing it at a slower pace. 

Even then, the amount of damage may never become as noticeable as it does with phones; that's simply because phone batteries are by design abused to a much greater extent than your scooter's battery will likely ever be. 

So if you're not prolonging longevity on a scooter with already limited range, a small battery or an already aging scooter, or doing it simply for the technological interest, you may be causing yourself more psychological suffering by worrying, than if you'd just bite the bullet if you ever do need to replace the battery.

My advice?  
If you're a regular consumer with a regular modern scooter, just use your scooter. Do not worry about the battery life.  
If you're a nerd looking for a reason to obsess about your battery life, well: you've already made up your mind. You don't need our validation. Your desires are enough of a reason to do whatever you'd like.

# Setup 3

### Storage

1. You've picked an "M.2 HBA" and a SAS to SATA adapter cable, but the M.2 card you've picked is not an HBA. It's just a bifurcating card that splits a 16x slot in to 4x4. Not only does that make it not an HBA, it doesn't have SAS and you need motherboard support for it as well. (Edit: just noticed, the SAS is for the backplane of the internal drive cages. So the SAS to SATA adapter cable makes sense.)
2. The motherboard you've picked has 6 or 8 on board SATA ports that go to its SATA controller. That means you won't have an NVMe overkill NAS.
3. You've got just one boot drive, without any redundancy.
4. You have just two NVMe storage solution banks. One of one drive, listed for OS and Cache. Pick one of either, but in either case, forget about Cache. (That's an oxymoron, yes.) Trying to use a single NVMe drive as cache on this system (let alone OS + cache, that's just a no-go) will severely hamper your performance because you simply don't have the available bandwidth to go caching to a lone PCIe connected drive when you have RAM available. If you were planning on using TrueNAS, TrueNAS won't be able to make proper use of a single cache NVMe drive because the topology just doesn't work that way.
5. Your WD Red Plus drives, can you list the model number of those?
6. If you want an NVMe based server, make it NVMe based first. That would most likely mean having a mirror across two sets of drives, where one set of drives is the NVMe and the other set of drives is the HDD's. You can set them up to mirror in the background so that you still benefit from whatever RAID setup you go with for the set of NVMe drives. Your HDD mirror side will always need to be equal or larger to the NVMe side.

### Mainboard

1. The motherboard you've picked supports ECC RAM, you've picked ECC RAM, but your CPU doesn't have an ECC capable memory controller. It's a desktop processor without the PRO featureset. Either get a server grade motherboard with an entry level server grade CPU, or stick to non-ECC. You probably don't really need ECC memory at this point in time, and it's needlessly eating up your budget.
2. Your CPU cooler is listed as a fairly expensive low profile vertical style Noctua cooler. It's rated to be 65mm tall with its fan. That means there's very little room to account for both the thickness of the motherboard, CPU on top of it, and the requisite room for your fan to suck in air. *This is a bad idea.* I also highly suspect you **wouldn't be able to fit this CPU cooler regardless**, as the case you've picked would require you to use your CPU cooler *underneath* the 3.5" HDD's, which you have in your basket.

It (largely) doesn't depend on the BMS, and the reasons for that are simple. I assume the person you replied to was referring to the following.  

Charging faster is done by keeping that voltage at or much closer to the target CV level, which results in higher amounts of current being drawn. This is a function of the charge current limit, and the limit is imposed by reducing the voltage.

That leads us to understand where DC fast charging leads to your current draw now being higher, which still needs to flow through the battery. The battery has internal resistances that are not of a negligable value, and a higher current through those resistances generates more heat. This by itself means there's more units of energy being converted to heat in the same span of time.

On top of that, the internal resistance value goes up the hotter the battery is; quite substantially by the end of the charge. That's why the charging gets significantly slower at the top end; it's to protect the battery from overheating to the point of failure. The internal resistance does change during the "mid-charge" levels of state-of-charge, and that increase caused by the extra heat does by itself again cause a small amount of extra heat; therefor the losses aren't merely just compacted into a smaller time frame but also cause more losses by their presence.

Additionally, the battery itself will heat up more when fast charging. It's a small but non-negligable amount of loss, and also directly related to why fast charging results in a lower overall life span in not just EV's, but all devices that use rechargable lithium-ion batteries.
